newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Observers arrive for risky Albania election.
newsitem.headline: Observers arrive for risky Albania election.

text.p: International observers began arriving in Albania on Tuesday ahead of a general election on Sunday, regarded as precarious as voting in Chechnya in January and in Bosnia last year.

The 54-nation Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), the Council of Europe, parliamentarians from across Europe and U.S. politicians will start fanning out across the former communist state on Friday to prepare to monitor the voting.
Despite concerns over security after dark on Election Day, Albanian President Sali Berisha has declined to issue a decree to close polling stations at 7 p.m. instead of 9 p.m., citing legal reasons.
"We would for security reasons prefer an earlier closing time. Problems tend to occur after hours of darkness," OSCE election coordinator Tony Welch said.
"It would be preferable to have observers back at their hotels," he told a news conference.
The vote, taking place just 13 months after a general election described as flawed by the OSCE, is being held under a state of emergency and a 10 p.m.-to-7 a.m. curfew.
Armed gangs roam freely in some parts of the country and shooting can be heard regularly after dark, even in the capital Tirana. Scores of people have died in the past week.
Some 450-500 official observers will only be able to visit a fraction of the 7,525 polling stations but officials believe their findings will be representational.
Up to 90 teams will stay in polling stations until the count is completed.
The total includes some 112 parliamentarians from 22 countries, and delegations from the European Union and the North Atlantic assembly.
This is the third election in which the OSCE has required armed escorts. "The OSCE had some escorts in Chechnya and in some areas of Bosnia last year," OSCE spokeswoman Melissa Fleming said.
A report on the conduct of the election will be put together by the OSCE and Council of Europe following the second round of voting on July 6.
The OSCE produced a critical report on Albania's third multi-party election last May but the Council of Europe's rival report was milder.
Opposition parties jumped on the OSCE findings to justify their boycott of the vote and the ruling Democrats cited the Council of Europe to uphold their landslide victory.

Council of Europe representative Egbert Aussems confirmed to reporters that this time there would be a joint report. "They will do their utmost to harmonise whatever they find into a global statement," he said.
A 7,000-strong, Italian-led international force was deployed in the Balkan state following days of armed rebellion in March, mainly in the south.

The force is expected to provide escorts to many of the observer teams but some national governments have refused to allow their soldiers into some of the more lawless zones of the mountainous country, diplomatic sources said.
In regions such as the barren northeast, observers will be accompanied by ECMM (European Community (Ed:correct) Monitoring Mission) representatives.

"Those people at the count will have a multinational escort close by," Welch said. "If the escorts think it is better for them to stay in the polling stations until dawn, then they will stay there until dawn."
Lieutenant Colonel Giovanni Bernardi told reporters two communications networks had been set up and were connected to protection force and OSCE headquarters ahead of Sunday's vote.

Once ballots have been counted, protocols bearing the results will be signed by electoral commissions on which the 10 main political parties are represented and will be handed into regional commission centres, then to the Central Electoral Commission based in Tirana.
First results are expected within 48 hours of polls closing.
